newsitem.title: MONACO: TENNIS-MUSTER, BECKER BEATEN IN MONTE CARLO. [CORRECTED 16:40 GMT]
newsitem.headline: TENNIS-MUSTER, BECKER BEATEN IN MONTE CARLO. [CORRECTED 16:40 GMT]

text.p: Thomas Muster's recent French jinx struck again on Tuesday when the Austrian world number two fell to Fabrice Santoro in straight sets at the Monte Carlo Open.

The 6-2 7-6 second round loss was all the more disappointing for Muster, beaten by another Frenchman, Cedric Pioline in Barcelona last week, as he had been chasing a record fourth win on the Monte Carlo clay.

Boris Becker also departed, beaten 1-6 6-3 7-6 by Italian Renzo Furlan, but his defeat in only his sixth match of the year on a surface which has still to yield him a tour title was more predictable than Muster's exit.

Muster, winner of the tournament for the past two years, has now lost three times in as many weeks on what used to be his favourite surface and can no longer claim to be the world's undisputed number one on clay.
Santoro, in fact, has become Muster's defeat "bete noire", beating him in their last two encounters.

"I had beaten him in the past and Iw what I had to do. I had to play short, deep, short, deep to wear him out. It worked and it's a great moment for me," said the Frenchman, ranked a lowly 90th in the world.
"It's always physically demanding to play against Thomas but I'm happy because I stay focused throughout."
After dropping the first set in half an hour, it seemed the Austrian, a winner in Key Biscayne this season, was regaining his composure when he broke Santoro for 3-1 in the second.
But the Frenchman fought back to level at 3-3 and, despite dropping his serve again in the ninth game, seized the initiative in the subseqent tie-break which ended with a Muster double fault.
Back on clay for the first time in a season so far marred by injury, Becker made a promising start but had difficulty adapting to the slow surface.
Currently ranked 12th in the world, the German only resumed playing in Tokyo last week after a two-month break because of a tendinitis. He had also complained of thigh pains in Tokyo.
"He was very good in the first set, especially at the net. Then he started playing poorly and I realised I only needed to play solid tennis," said Furlan, currently 65th on the computer.

"It's a big disappointment because I was so close to winning but to be so close to win when I served so poorly was a surprise," said Becker, who could only manage a lacklustre first serve percentage of 38 percent.

Spain's numerous clay court experts had no such problems with Alberto Costa, the winner in Barcelona on Monday, Francisco Clavet, Alberto Berasategui, Felix Mantilla and Alex Corretja all scoring straight set victories.
